summary: Initial discovery for migrating from OpenAI-hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated. Focus on compatibility (OpenAI API parity, vLLM/TGI), eval parity, expected latency and throughput, security/VPC requirements, and next-step benchmarking/pilot. Customer wants cost predictability and data isolation for production robotics workloads.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Priya: Hi all. Nice to meet you. We'll run through how Redwood Dedicated works and dig into the specifics around your OpenAI migration.
[00:13] Samir: Thanks. I'm Samir, CTO at Haven. Quick context: we run a fleet of edge robots and use LLMs for on-device planning/assistant features. Right now most of our models are served through OpenAI for R&D and early prod, but costs are spiking and we need more control — data residency and latency predictability.
[00:29] Emily: And from platform side, we evaluate model parity — outputs must match our existing evals for safety and accuracy. Small quality regressions are risky.
[00:38] Liam: I'm here for infra/ops — network, VPC, and how Dedicated will sit in our AWS account.
[00:44] Jordan: Totally. Goal today: map your current stack, compatibility questions (OpenAI API, vLLM/TGI), perf expectations, and the security constraints to see if Dedicated or Private is the right fit.
[00:55] Priya: Before we dig in, can you outline current traffic patterns and models? e.g., typical seq lengths, tokens per request, p95 latency target, qps?
[01:05] Samir: Sure. Most calls are chat-style instructions with 256–512 tokens per request. p95 latency target is ~250–300ms for short-form planning requests. Peak QPS is around 40–60 for a single region, but bursts hit 120 qps for short windows during fleet sync. We also use embeddings for retrieval — about 2M embeddings per day.
[01:28] Priya: Got it. And are you calling OpenAI APIs directly from edge devices or via your backend?
[01:32] Emily: Backend only. We proxy everything through our platform so we can do caching and safety filters. We also experimented with vLLM on prem for some test workloads but found engineering fragility—ops complexity, memory fragmentation, and rollout drift.
[01:46] Jordan: That's super common. One of the things Redwood Dedicated provides is a managed runtime tuned for continuous batching and KV cache reuse so you get both cost savings and predictable latency without the vLLM operational burden.
[02:00] Samir: High level question: how compatible is Redwood with the OpenAI API surface? We have hundreds of endpoints and some code paths do model switching dynamically.
[02:09] Priya: Short answer: we provide OpenAI-compatible endpoints for common patterns — completions/chat/embeddings — and support function-calling semantics. There are edge cases around streaming chunking and some beta endpoints; we can map those during the pilot.
[02:23] Samir: And models? We currently use GPT-4o-ish families and a mix of open models for embeddings. We also run some TGI-hosted fine-tuned variants.
[02:33] Priya: We host a catalog of verified open models and also provide model variants with quantization profiles. For TGI/vLLM artifacts, we can ingest weights provided they're compatible — but there are nuances: custom kernel paths, attention implementations, and KV cache formats can vary. We usually recommend running a short eval parity suite during onboarding to validate outputs.
[02:53] Emily: Eval parity is critical for us. What does that suite look like? We have safety tests, hallucination checks, and behavior on corner cases.
[03:02] Priya: We typically run a 3k-10k prompt test set you provide. We'll run it against your production model on OpenAI and the candidate on Redwood Dedicated and provide diff metrics: token-level divergence, top-k output variation, perplexity proxies, and task-specific metrics you care about. Can also hook in your automated eval harness.
[03:20] Samir: And what's the expected divergence window? In past migrations to other runtimes we saw small but meaningful differences — sometimes a policy filter flagged outputs differently.
[03:30] Jordan: Most parity diffs are small if model weights are identical and quantization/profile choices are compatible. When differences show up it's often due to attention kernel differences or subtle tokenization mismatches. Priya can speak to mitigation.
[03:42] Priya: Right — we compare tokenization step-by-step, and if needed we can run the model in higher-precision mode for the eval. We also keep a rollback path to the hosted variant during rollout. The key is an iterative eval+threshold gating for canary.
[03:57] Liam: From ops: how does Dedicated integrate with our VPC? We need private subnets, specific firewall rules, and egress control. Also KMS for key management.
[04:07] Priya: Dedicated runs in your AWS account (or a managed account depending on the engagement). You can choose VPC peering or VPC endpoint models. We support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest, and audit logs stream to your CloudWatch/S3. We'll need your network diagram and any strict egress rules to plan NAT/ENI placement.
[04:25] Samir: Do you support SSO/SAML and RBAC for team management?
[04:29] Jordan: Yes, SSO (SAML/Okta) and role-based access controls are supported. We also do per-route tokenization cost breakdowns and can set quotas.
[04:38] Emily: Cost question: our current OpenAI spend is high; can Redwood Dedicated be predictably cheaper? We're looking for committed capacity pricing but want to understand unit token economics.
[04:48] Jordan: Dedicated pricing is typically a reserved capacity contract. You get predictable throughput and lower per-token cost due to batching, KV cache reuse, and quantization. We'll run a sizing exercise to recommend GPU pool size and reserve tiers.
[05:00] Priya: One more item — latency. You mentioned p95 250–300ms. For that profile we recommend a mix of lower-latency GPU models for the short requests and offload long-form jobs to a separate pool. Continuous batching helps but adds scheduling latency; we tune batch window and tail latency to meet p95 SLOs.
[05:18] Samir: Can you give a rough example: what does 250ms p95 look like for a 256-token request on a T4 vs an A100?
[05:26] Priya: T4s are trickier for 250ms p95 at 256 tokens for larger models — you'd probably need an A100 or H100-backed pool for that SLO, or use a smaller quantized model that still meets accuracy. We'll show options after we see your benchmark prompts.
[05:40] Liam: About embeddings: we need ~2M/day — is there a different path for batch embedding jobs vs realtime?
[05:47] Priya: Yes, batch embedding workloads are great candidates for separate worker pools or autoscale policies to save cost. We support embedding-only nodes and async batch endpoints.
[05:55] Emily: Security/compliance: we're SOC2 in progress, and our customers ask about auditability. How do we get logs and retention?
[06:02] Jordan: We provide audit logs, request/response level tracing for debugging (can be redacted), and configurable retention. For enterprise customers we can extend retention as an add-on. We also support dedicated control plane options for Private deployments.
[06:15] Samir: On model ownership: we may want to bring our fine-tuned TGI artifacts. You said ingesting weights might have nuances — do you convert to a Redwood-optimized runtime? Is that a one-time conversion?
[06:27] Priya: We do a conversion step — kernel selection, quantization profiles, and build a serving artifact. It's repeatable but you should expect a validation window. We keep the original weights and can restore if needed. For some TGI variants we need small adapter scripts if their attention or positional encodings deviate.
[06:42] Samir: What about operator tooling — rollout controls, canary, automatic fallback to hosted model?
[06:49] Jordan: Yes — rollouts, canary percentages, automatic rollback on error budget breach, and policy-based routing (region, cost-tier). We also have perf traces and token-level cost dashboards in the console.
[07:00] Emily: For the eval parity suite, will Redwood run the tests or do we run locally? We prefer to keep ground-truth runs inside our environment for sensitive prompts.
[07:08] Priya: We can support both. You can run your eval harness against a self-hosted test instance in your account, and we can run parallel runs on our staging environment and exchange diffs.
[07:18] Samir: Latency for edge devices is sensitive — sometimes we need sub-200ms for short commands. Is edge deployment (on-prem) part of the Private options?
[07:27] Jordan: We offer Private (VPC/on-prem) with a control plane that's customer-managed. For strict sub-200ms you might consider local inference instances near the edge or a hybrid: Dedicated in-region pools for low-latency plus on-device tiny models for micro commands.
[07:41] Liam: Networking specifics — we have strict egress via a NAT and proxy; does Redwood require outbound internet from the compute nodes?
[07:49] Priya: For Dedicated inside your account, outbound egress can be controlled. We'll align with your security team. Some image pulls and control-plane interactions need limited connectivity during setup; we can discuss an air-gapped flow if needed.
[08:02] Samir: Ok. Can we talk about timeline? We have a quarter deadline to cut OpenAI dependence for certain features. Realistic pilot timeline?
[08:10] Jordan: Typical pilot runs 4–8 weeks: week 0-1 onboarding & sizing, week 2 run eval parity + perf benchmarks, weeks 3-4 iterate on tuning, then a canary rollout. If there's urgency we can compress with dedicated engineering resources.
[08:24] Emily: For the benchmark, will Redwood's SEs run the full end-to-end tests including network hop emulation?
[08:30] Priya: We can run both internal benchmarks and, importantly, run tests inside your AWS account so network/hop emulation is realistic. We'll need your ops access or a scoped IAM role.
[08:40] Jordan: Quick note — we've seen customers hit a surprise cost when they don't adopt prefix/KV caching patterns. Are you currently doing any prefix caching?
[08:48] Emily: We cache at the retrieval layer but not at the prefix/KV level from the model. That's an area we wanted to explore.
[08:55] Priya: Implementing KV cache reuse can drastically reduce token compute for repeated contexts, especially for chat-style sessions. We'll include recommendations in the sizing worksheet.
[09:03] Samir: Anything else we should know?
[09:06] Jordan: I think we've covered core items. Let's recap next steps.
[09:10] Priya: Recap: Jordan will send pricing + reserved sizing worksheet; Emily will share sample prompts and eval metrics; Liam will share network constraints; Priya will schedule the perf benchmark. We'll aim for initial benchmark week of 2026-03-09.
[09:25] Samir: That sounds good. One more Q — what about fallback to OpenAI if Dedicated has an outage?
[09:31] Jordan: We support policy-based fallback to hosted endpoints (OpenAI or Redwood hosted). You can configure automatic failover with percentage-based fallback and circuit breakers.
[09:40] Liam: Great. I might have some follow-ups about IAM and ENI limits.
[09:44] Emily: We'll get the prompt set over by Thursday.
[09:47] Jordan: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll send the materials and calendar invites for the benchmark scheduling.
[09:53] Samir: Thanks. Appreciate the clarity.
[09:55] [call ends]

Notes: transcription contains some mis-heard words ("Red wood"/"Redwod" in a couple of places in the auto-transcript), occasional filler words preserved. References to external artifacts: pricing deck link (sent after call), dedicated sizing worksheet (template), SOC2/security package (link).
